title: DDR1 sustains ferroptosis resistance in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma via SLC40A1-mediated iron homeostasis
abstract: Integrated single-cell transcriptomics and clinical analyses reveal elevated DDR1 expression in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) tissues, which correlates with poor prognosis. Mechanistically, collagen-activated Discoidin Domain Receptor 1 (DDR1) recruits SHC1 to activate the MAPK/ERK pathway, thereby driving transcriptional upregulation of SLC40A1 via the ERK-MYC axis. SLC40A1, encoding an iron exporter, reduces intracellular labile iron pools, thereby suppressing lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. Consequently, DDR1 overexpression confers resistance to dihydroartemisinin (DHA)-induced ferroptosis in PDAC cells, characterized by diminished ROS accumulation, mitochondrial shrinkage, and cristae loss. Conversely, DDR1 knockdown or pharmacological inhibition (Dasatinib) sensitizes PDAC cells to DHA. Crucially, combining Dasatinib and DHA treatment synergistically inhibits tumor growth in vivo by reactivating ferroptosis, as evidenced by increased 4-HNE accumulation and decreased Ki67 expression. These findings identify DDR1 as a key regulator of iron metabolism and ferroptosis in PDAC, suggesting that dual targeting of DDR1 and ferroptosis represents a promising therapeutic strategy.

title: SETDB1 cooperates with the CRL4B complex to promote colorectal cancer tumorigenesis by disrupting circadian rhythm
abstract: The circadian rhythm is an intrinsic, self-regulatory physiological system in organisms that is hierarchically governed by core clock genes. Dysregulation of this rhythm is closely associated with tumor progression. However, the specific molecular mechanisms underlying circadian rhythm disruption-mediated colorectal cancer (CRC) remain largely elusive. The histone methyltransferase SET domain bifurcated 1 (SETDB1) exerts oncogenic functions in multiple solid tumors, prompting this study to investigate the molecular mechanisms through which SETDB1 regulates CRC progression. Our results demonstrate that SETDB1 acts as an oncogene in CRC by interacting with the Cullin 4B-RING E3 ligase (CRL4B) complex to enhance cancer cell proliferation, invasion, and stemness maintenance. Specifically, SETDB1 and the CRL4B complex assemble into a transcriptional repressor complex that binds to the promoters of core clock genes, such as PER3 and CRY1, to repress their transcription, thereby disrupting cellular circadian rhythms and ultimately accelerating CRC cell proliferation and metastasis. Collectively, our findings elucidate the pivotal role of the SETDB1/CRL4B complex in CRC pathogenesis and provide a potential therapeutic strategy targeting SETDB1 for patients with CRC with high CUL4B expression.

title: Synonymous codon usage shapes ERα function through specialized translational programs during breast cancer progression
abstract: Long considered neutral, synonymous codon usage is increasingly recognized as a regulatory layer of mRNA translation. Proteins expressed during proliferation are translated from mRNAs with codon compositions distinct from those encoding proteins in differentiated states, suggesting the existence of specialized translational programs. In hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, estrogen receptor-alpha (ERα/ESR1) acts both as a driver of proliferation and as a maintainer of luminal identity, making its translational regulation particularly relevant. Here, we show that the transition of breast cancer cells from quiescent, differentiated states towards proliferative, less differentiated phenotypes, is accompanied by a systematic shift from G/C3- to A/U3-biased codon usage. ERα coding sequence architecture mirrors these translational programs through both global codon composition and position-dependent codon patterns. These features influence translational efficiency and likely modulate co-translational folding dynamics, thereby adjusting receptor abundance and functional outputs according to the prevailing translational program. Consistent with their functional importance, synonymous codon choices are subject to increased selective constraints within regions encoding structural and functional domains. Using engineer synonymous ERα variants, we demonstrate that codon usage fine-tunes receptor function across distinct cellular states. Together, our findings identify synonymous codon usage as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking translational programs to ERα expression and function.

title: Phylogenetic and phylodynamic approaches to understanding the evolution of non-small cell lung cancer using single-cell sequencing
abstract: Abstract Characterizing the genealogy of tumor cells and their population dynamics is central to our understanding of the evolution of cancer. While direct monitoring of the tumor evolutionary process is impractical, we leverage advances in phylogenetics and phylodynamics to explore the evolutionary dynamics of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) using single-cell whole exome sequencing data from 351 tumor cells across 11 NSCLC patients, predominantly focusing on the primary tumors and early stages of NSCLC. Our results reveal distinct phylogenetic tree shapes and evolutionary trajectories across different stages of NSCLC evolution. However, this intricate and multi-phase evolutionary process cannot be fully elucidated by current tumor models. Herein, we hypothesize that tumors progress through the following phases: (1) an initial rapid expansion through Big Bang-like growth, (2) a prolonged plateau period of non-progression with possible accumulation of neutral substitutions, (3) a subsequent phase where adaptive substitutions accumulate gradually, (4) a bottleneck event where selectively advantageous subclones acquire invasive capabilities (characterized by a pattern of punctuated evolution), and, potentially, a rapid expansion leading to metastasis. This work highlights the use of single-cell phylogenetics and phylodynamics for interpreting the evolution of NSCLC, with potential in predicting cancer progression, resistance mechanisms, and treatment response.

title: KAT5-mediated HSPA1A lactylation drives immunotherapy resistance by inhibiting STAT1 degradation in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Immunotherapy has shown promising efficacy in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), yet its clinical benefits remain limited due to immune evasion. Lactate accumulation in the tumor microenvironment has been found to facilitate immune evasion through protein lactylation. However, the key lactylated substrates and mechanisms driving immune evasion remain undefined. Here, we show that HSPA1A lactylation at lysine 108 (K108) by KAT5 drives CD8⁺ T cell dysfunction and immunotherapy resistance via the STAT1/PD-L1 axis in ESCC. Mechanistically, K108 lactylation enhances HSPA1A binding to STAT1, protecting STAT1 from TRIM25-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. This stabilization promotes STAT1 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, leading to transcriptional upregulation of PD-L1 and subsequent immune evasion. Collectively, these findings highlight the pivotal role of HSPA1A lactylation in facilitating immune evasion via the STAT1/PD-L1 axis, suggesting a potential target for improving immunotherapy efficacy in ESCC.

title: KIFC1 engages RUNX2/TGF-β signaling to promote lung cancer bone metastasis via disrupting bone homeostasis
abstract: Bone metastasis affects 30-40% of lung cancer patients, markedly reducing survival and quality of life, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Comparative transcriptomic profiling of primary lung tumors and paired bone metastases revealed pronounced KIFC1 enrichment in metastatic lesions, which correlated with poor bone metastasis-free survival. Functionally, KIFC1 enhanced lung cancer cell migration and adhesion toward osteoblast-like cells and upregulated the bone-homing factors CXCR4 and OPN. KIFC1 promoted osteoclast recruitment and differentiation while suppressing osteogenic differentiation, thereby disrupting bone homeostasis. Mechanistically, KIFC1 associated with RUNX2 through its C-terminal motor domain and promoted RUNX2 nuclear accumulation in a motor activity-, microtubule-, and importin-dependent manner. Nuclear RUNX2 directly activated TGFB1 transcription, resulting in preferential activation of the TGF-β/SMAD3 signaling pathway. Genetic silencing of RUNX2 or pharmacological inhibition of SMAD3 largely abrogated KIFC1-mediated pro-metastatic and pro-osteolytic effects. In vivo, KIFC1 knockdown reduced intraosseous tumor burden and alleviated trabecular bone loss, whereas KIFC1 overexpression exacerbated osteolytic lesions, which were mitigated by disrupting RUNX2/TGF-β/SMAD3 signaling. Collectively, our findings identify KIFC1-mediated RUNX2 nuclear transport as a previously unrecognized upstream regulatory mechanism that activates the TGF-β/SMAD3 axis during lung cancer bone metastasis, which provides a conceptual framework for the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: A positive feedback loop between YTHDC1 and EP300 drives multiple myeloma tumorigenesis
abstract: N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A), the most prevalent internal RNA modification in mammals, regulates key cellular processes through writer, eraser, and reader proteins. Recent studies have emerged that dysregulation of m 6 A modifiers promotes tumorigenesis by altering RNA metabolism. However, the role of m 6 A in multiple myeloma (MM) remains enigmatic. Here, we identify YTHDC1, a nuclear m 6 A reader, as a key oncogenic factor in MM. YTHDC1 is upregulated in MM cells and associated with poor prognosis. Functional studies reveal that YTHDC1 facilitates MM cell growth and survival in an m 6 A-dependent manner. Mechanistically, YTHDC1 directly binds m 6 A-modified EP300 mRNA and enhances its stability and expression. In turn, p300 activates YTHDC1 transcription via H3K27ac deposition and IRF3/IRF4 recruitment, establishing a self-reinforcing feedback loop. This interplay between RNA m 6 A methylation and histone H3K27 acetylation contributes to MM pathogenesis. Our findings highlight the YTHDC1-EP300 axis as a promising target for therapeutic intervention.

title: Metabolites and cancer metastasis
abstract: Over the past decades, metastasis research has largely emphasized genetic and epigenetic regulators. Emerging evidence indicates that metabolites-including sugars (glucose, fructose), antioxidant vitamins, glutathione, lipids (palmitic acid, cholesterol), and amino acids (glutamine, aspartate, BCAAs)-can critically influence metastasis in a context-dependent manner by driving or restraining progression via metabolic reprogramming and signaling modulation. This review examines how cancer cells re-modulate core metabolic pathways to adapt and metastasize, summarizes how endogenous metabolites, dietary bioactive compounds, metabolic toxins, and pharmacological agents regulate metastasis, and discusses new concepts and perspectives on metabolic regulation of tumor metastasis, and outlines future directions in metabolite-driven tumor metastasis. The metabolic dependencies of metastasis provide a rational basis for intervention through integrated nutritional and therapeutic strategies.

title: SPTLC2-driven sphingolipid reprogramming of neutrophils impairs anti-tumour immunity and drives liver cancer progression
abstract: Liver cancer exhibits limited and heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint blockade, underscoring the need to elucidate tumour microenvironmental mechanisms sustaining immune dysfunction. Here, we integrated single-cell transcriptomic annotation with BayesPrism deconvolution across multiple bulk cohorts and combined these analyses with in vivo liver cancer models, functional assays, and mechanistic investigations to define tumour-associated neutrophil (TAN) programmes linked to clinical outcome. We identified a neutrophil subset characterized by elevated sphingolipid metabolism as the predominant poor-prognosis signature, with SPTLC2 serving as the key molecular marker. High SPTLC2 expression defining this sphingolipid metabolism-high neutrophil population correlated significantly with advanced disease stage, inferior overall survival, and increased tumour infiltration. Tumour cell co-culture induced SPTLC2 upregulation and enhanced sphingolipid metabolic activity in neutrophils. Functional assays verified that myriocin, an SPTLC2 inhibitor, suppressed the proliferation and metastasis of Liver cancer cells and remodelled the antitumour immune function of neutrophils. Myriocin attenuated neutrophil sphingolipid metabolism and restored ROS production and neutrophil extracellular trap (NETosis) formation, revealing a critical regulatory role for sphingolipid metabolism in neutrophil-mediated innate immunity, as corroborated by single-cell analyses showing impaired innate immune function in sphingolipid metabolism-high neutrophils. Mechanistically, we uncovered an SPTLC2-dependent sphingolipid-lipid raft checkpoint that remodels plasma membrane microdomains to constrain neutrophil anti-tumour effector functions. Specifically, myriocin restored NOX2-dependent ROS generation by reducing ceramide accumulation in lipid rafts, thereby facilitating p47 phox -p22 phox interaction and productive NOX2 complex assembly in tumour-conditioned neutrophils. Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized immunometabolic axis governing TAN dysfunction in liver cancer, establish SPTLC2 as a rational combinatorial target for cancer immunotherapy, and highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting sphingolipid metabolism to restore neutrophil-mediated antitumour immunity and restrain hepatocellular carcinoma progression.

title: ACTB promotes ESCC progression by regulating the AKT–mTOR signaling pathway through an m6A-dependent mechanism
abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a highly aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis, and the upstream regulatory mechanisms driving oncogenic signaling remain insufficiently defined. In this study, we identify a previously unrecognized nuclear function of the cytoskeletal protein ACTB in promoting ESCC progression. We show that ACTB translocates to the nucleus and directly binds to the promoter of the m6A reader gene YTHDC2, transcriptionally activating its expression. YTHDC2, in turn, binds to m6A-modified sites on AKT mRNA, preventing its degradation and enhancing its stability. This results in sustained activation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway, a key oncogenic cascade that promotes tumor growth and survival. Integrated CUT&Tag and RNA-seq analyses revealed a direct ACTB-YTHDC2 transcriptional axis, while RNA immunoprecipitation and MeRIP-qPCR confirmed YTHDC2-AKT interaction via m6A recognition. Functional assays in ESCC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and xenograft mouse models demonstrated that both ACTB and YTHDC2 are essential for ESCC proliferation and tumorigenicity. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of mTOR with rapamycin effectively suppressed ACTB-driven tumor phenotypes in vitro and in vivo, supporting the therapeutic relevance of this signaling axis. Together, our findings define a novel ACTB-YTHDC2-AKT-mTOR regulatory network that integrates transcriptional and epitranscriptomic control in ESCC. This study reveals a noncanonical nuclear role for ACTB and identifies a mechanistically tractable pathway that may be exploited for targeted therapy in ACTB-driven esophageal cancer.

title: Nuclear cathepsin L induces DNA damage by regulating DNA repair factors in ovarian cancer
abstract: Resistance to PARP inhibitors (PARPi) remains a major clinical challenge in ovarian cancer (OC), emphasizing the need for novel strategies to enhance therapeutic efficiency. Our previous work revealed that the antimalarial drug quinacrine (QC) can be repurposed to induce cell death in OC by promoting lysosomal release of active cathepsin L (CTSL). Building on these outcomes, we investigated whether QC-activated CTSL influences DNA damage and homologous recombination (HR) repair in OC cells. Our experimental evidence shows that QC-activated CTSL downregulates key DNA repair proteins RAD51 and 53BP1, leading to impaired HR repair and increased DNA damage. Importantly, genetic knockdown of CTSL significantly reduced QC-induced DNA damage, confirming the CTSL plays a direct functional role in this process. We also found out that the response of combined QC and PARPi differs in models. CTSL was translocated to the nucleus (nCTSL) in responsive patient-derived ascitic (PDA) and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) spheroids. Contrarily, non-responsive models did not have nuclear CTSL. Mechanically, QC could not suppress CRM1/XPO1 nuclear export receptor in non-responsive cells, leading to continued export of CTSL from the nucleus. To address this, we have used the CRM1 inhibitor KPT-8602, which restored nuclear retention of CTSL. This led to enhanced therapeutic synergy with PARPi and overcame resistance in QC-treated PDA 3D-spheroids. Consistent with these findings, QC reduced tumor burden in both the cell-derived OVCAR-5 xenograft and PDX-PH070 models that showed QC-induced nCTSL, but not in the non-responsive PDX-PH095 model. However, in additional non-responsive PDX models (PH747 and PH081), treatment with QC and KPT-8602 substantially reduced tumor burden. Collectively, our results confirm a critical role for nuclear CTSL in QC-induced DNA damage and identify nCTSL as a possible predictive biomarker of therapeutic response. These results suggest that combining QC with PARPi or CRM1 inhibitors represents a promising strategy to overcome PARPi resistance in OC.

title: TFAM loss drives oxaliplatin resistance by linking mtDNA release to STING–TBK1-mediated lysophagy
abstract: Acquired resistance to oxaliplatin (Oxa) represents a major clinical challenge in the treatment of colorectal cancer (CRC). Lysosomes are intracellular degradative organelles that enable cancer cells to adapt to metabolic and environmental stress; however, their precise regulatory roles in drug resistance remain poorly understood. Here, we report that lysosomal damage and its selective autophagic clearance (lysophagy) occur frequently in both Oxa-treated CRC cells and Oxa-resistant (OxaR) CRC cells. Through quantitative proteomics, we identified the significant downregulation of mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) as a key event in Oxa-treated and OxaR cells. Mechanistically, Oxa-induced TFAM loss leads to mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) leakage into the cytosol, which activates the STING-TBK1 signaling axis. This pathway subsequently enhances lysophagic flux, providing cancer cells with a survival advantage under Oxa stress. Crucially, pharmacological inhibition of TBK1 abrogates this adaptive lysophagy, restoring Oxa sensitivity and suppressing tumor growth in both xenograft and patient-derived organoid models. Collectively, our study reveals a novel TFAM-mtDNA-STING-TBK1 signaling axis that promotes chemoresistance through the co-option of lysophagy, highlighting TBK1 as a viable therapeutic target to overcome Oxa resistance in CRC.

title: KDM4A drives TGCT metastasis by inducing focal adhesion disassembly via STAT1-mediated CCL3 transcriptional activation
abstract: Dysregulation of histone demethylation is a pivotal epigenetic event driving malignant tumor progression. Thus, it is critical to understand the downstream signaling pathways that govern dysregulation of histone demethylation. Here, we identified KDM4A as the exclusively and significantly up-regulated member in testicular germ cell tumors (TGCTs) through a pan-family expression screen of histone demethylases (KDM1-8 and JMJD6) using the GEPIA database. KDM4A knockdown markedly inhibits TGCT cell migration and invasion in vitro, and metastatic potential in vivo. Mechanistically, KDM4A induces H3K9me3 demethylation at the CCL3 promoter, thereby restoring chromatin accessibility to facilitate STAT1-dependent CCL3 transcriptional activation, which activates the PI3K/AKT pathway, ultimately promoting focal adhesion turnover and enhancing cellular invasiveness. Furthermore, in a lung metastasis model, KDM4A significantly promoted distal colonization of TGCT in a CCL3-dependent manner. Summary, our findings reveal that KDM4A is a critical epigenetic regulator of TGCT metastasis, driving tumor progression via the STAT1-dependent CCL3 transcriptional activation, which promotes focal adhesion turnover by PI3K/AKT axis. Hence, targeting KDM4A may be a promising therapeutic strategy for improving the clinical prognosis of patients with metastatic TGCT.

title: Correction: C/EBPδ-Slug-Lox1 axis promotes metastasis of lung adenocarcinoma via oxLDL uptake
SMCO2 inhibits ferroptosis through the VDAC1–STAT3 axis by modulating MAM homeostasis in ovarian cancer
abstract: This study identifies the previously uncharacterised transmembrane protein SMCO2 as a broadly upregulated factor in multi-organ adenocarcinomas and defines it as a novel mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membrane (MAM) structural and signalling integrator. Adenocarcinoma cells maintain metabolic adaptability and resist cell death through enhanced mitochondrial-endoplasmic reticulum communication; however, the core transmembrane regulation node that regulates this process is still unclear. Our article proves that SMCO2 interacts with VDAC1, enhances its association with STAT3, and promotes mitochondrial localisation and S727 phosphorylation of STAT3. The SMCO2-driven VDAC1–STAT3 axis modulates mitochondrial Ca² + signalling, oxidative stress homoeostasis, and pivotal ferroptosis-associated networks, ultimately conferring ferroptosis resistance on tumour cells. Targeting SMCO2 or the VDAC1/STAT3 pathway can effectively restore ferroptosis sensitivity. Overall, our study confirms that SMCO2 is a transmembrane regulatory factor and reveals that the MAM-STAT3 axis, as a new mechanism, links metabolic adaptation to adenocarcinoma cell death resistance and has potential therapeutic significance.

title: Adrenomedullin 2 drives intratumoral cancer cell invasion, intravasation and metastasis
abstract: Cancer cell intravasation requires both directed invasion toward the vasculature and access to functional blood vessels that act as intravasation sites. Using intravital video microscopy, we identified the peptide hormone adrenomedullin 2 (ADM2) as a critical regulator of this process. ADM2 was selectively upregulated in a highly invasive subpopulation of cancer cells that localize near blood vessels and actively drive intravasation. Knockdown of ADM2 significantly impaired intratumoral cancer cell invasion and intravasation in a chicken embryo metastasis model and in vitro. ADM2-deficient tumors exhibited reduced vascularization, limiting the availability of competent intravasation sites. Moreover, loss of ADM2 suppressed the formation of invasive metastatic lesions, indicating a requirement for ADM2 at multiple stages of the metastatic cascade. Consistently, targeting ADM2 in a mouse metastasis model inhibited the development of large intratumoral blood vessels and reduced metastasis. Collectively, these findings establish ADM2 as a previously unrecognized regulator of tumor-vascular interactions and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target to simultaneously disrupt invasion, vascular support, and metastatic dissemination.

title: PTK7 scaffolds DNA-PKcs to promote DNA damage response and immune evasion in triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: Membrane proteins with nuclear localization often exert non-canonical functions. PTK7, an evolutionarily conserved pseudokinase and a prominent therapeutic target, is primarily recognized for its cell-surface signaling; however, its intracellular role in tumor biology remains unclear. Here, we identify a previously unrecognized role of PTK7 in coordinating DNA damage response and tumor immune response in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Mechanistically, PTK7 translocates to the nucleus where it associates with DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PKcs), acting as a molecular scaffold to enhance its kinase activation and facilitate non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) repair. Loss of PTK7 impaired DNA-PKcs-associated non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) repair, increased double-strand breaks, and subsequent activation of the STING-IFN axis. Furthermore, PTK7 deficiency significantly sensitizes TNBC tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy in vivo. Clinically, high PTK7 expression correlates with suppressed immune signatures and poor immunotherapy response in TNBC patients. Together, our findings uncover a PTK7-associated DNA repair and immune-evasion program in TNBC and nominate PTK7 as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for improving immunotherapy response.

title: Correction: Targeting surface nucleolin induces autophagy-dependent cell death in pancreatic cancer via AMPK activation
TNFα-driven epigenetic upregulation of TIGIT creates a targetable vulnerability in tumors
abstract: T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT) is a key inhibitory receptor on cytotoxic lymphocytes, yet the mechanisms governing its context-dependent upregulation in tumors remain poorly defined. Here, we identify tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) signaling as an upstream driver of TIGIT expression. Integrated analyses of patient transcriptomic datasets revealed a consistent positive association between TNFα pathway activity and TIGIT expression across multiple cancer types, with strong concordance in melanoma and prognostic relevance in kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Mechanistically, TNFα directly induced TIGIT expression in natural killer cells via TNFR2 signaling, increasing chromatin accessibility at distal TIGIT enhancers and promoting NF-κB and AP-1 recruitment together with BRD4 and P300. Functionally, combined anti-TNFα and anti-TIGIT treatment suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival more effectively than either monotherapy in murine melanoma and colon cancer models. These findings define a TNFα-TNFR2-enhancer axis controlling TIGIT expression and provide a mechanistic rationale for dual TNFα and TIGIT targeting in inflamed tumors.

title: Methylation-driven SOX18 nuclear translocation by IGF2BP1-stabilized METTL21A promotes lymphatic metastasis in gastric cancer
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is frequently associated with lymph node metastasis, which contributes to a poor prognosis; however, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identify the N6-methyladenosine (m⁶A) reader IGF2BP1 as a critical driver of lymphatic metastasis in GC. IGF2BP1 is significantly upregulated in GC tissues with lymph node metastasis and is correlated with adverse clinical outcomes. Mechanistically, IGF2BP1 binds to the m⁶A-modified 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of METTL21A mRNA, thereby enhancing its mRNA stability and expression levels. METTL21A, a non-histone lysine methyltransferase, interacts with and methylates the transcription factor SOX18, facilitating its nuclear translocation without altering protein stability. Once in the nucleus, SOX18 directly activates the transcription of CXCL12. Secreted CXCL12 promotes lymphangiogenesis and facilitates lymphatic metastasis through CXCR4 signaling. Functionally, both IGF2BP1 and METTL21A enhance tube formation and migration of lymphatic endothelial cells and promote lymphatic metastasis in GC. Notably, METTL21A knockout abolishes IGF2BP1-induced lymphangiogenesis, whereas SOX18 depletion eliminates the pro-lymphangiogenic effects of IGF2BP1. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized signaling axis-IGF2BP1-METTL21A-SOX18-CXCL12-that links m⁶A-dependent post-transcriptional regulation with methylation-dependent transcriptional activation, offering potential therapeutic targets for the prevention of lymphatic metastasis in gastric cancer.

title: Dynamic remodeling of the KRAS interactome by direct RAS inhibitors with distinct mechanism of action reveals convergent responses
abstract: KRAS is mutated in 30% of all human cancers. Small molecule inhibitors targeting KRAS with distinct mechanisms-of-action and variable specificities have entered the clinic, but their full effect on the RAS signaling network remains unclear. Here, we described the impact of RAS inhibition on the KRAS interactome using Proximity-dependent Biotin Identification. Two inhibitors were used: panRAS-ON, which forms a ternary complex between cyclophilin and RAS in the GTP-bound state; panKRAS-off, which binds to the KRAS switch II pocket. RAS inhibitors were found to significantly alter 16.5% of proteins in proximity to KRAS. Despite their distinct modality, the KRAS inhibitors induced highly correlated changes in the KRAS interactomes. Among KRAS-proximal proteins, Afadin was highly affected by RAS inhibition. AFDN is a key regulator of cell motility, invasion, and metastasis. Analysis of AFDN phosphorylation revealed that AKT only partially modulates p-Ser1718, while KRAS inhibition sufficiently abolished EGF-mediated AFDN phosphorylation. Silencing AFDN in a KRAS-driven non-small cell lung cancer model abolished chemotaxis and disrupted directional migration in an EGF-driven wound healing model. We demonstrated that KRAS is a central node in regulating growth factor-induced cell migration, and that KRAS inhibition plays a broader role than MAPK-mediated cell proliferation and survival.

title: Dual novel compounds destroy mitochondrial morphology and function to treat glioblastoma by promoting the p62-mediated protein degradation of mitochondrial respiratory chain complex
abstract: Therapeutic efficacy of temozolomide (TMZ) remains limited, and GBM patients generally experience poor outcomes due to the presence of multiple mechanisms of TMZ resistance. Previously, we developed two novel compounds: EPIC-1027, which targets HOTAIR/PRC2 complex, and EPIC-1042, which disrupts interaction between PTRF and CAV1. In this study, we aim to establish a novel combinatorial strategy for GBM by targeting mitochondrial function. Proteomics was employed to evaluate global protein alterations induced by EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042. Super-resolution microscopy and transmission electron microscopy were used to characterize changes in mitochondrial morphology. Metabolic flux analysis was performed to assess alterations in cellular energy metabolism following combined treatment. An intracranial GBM model was established to validate the anti-GBM efficacy of EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 in vivo. Combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 reduced the abundance of respiratory chain complex proteins by promoting p62-dependent protein degradation, resulting in severe mitochondrial damage. Both glycolytic activity and oxidative phosphorylation were markedly suppressed following EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 treatment. In vitro, EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 exerted a synergistic inhibitory effect on GBM cell proliferation and significantly induced apoptosis in an MGMT-independent manner. In vivo, combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 significantly attenuated tumor growth and prolonged survival in mice bearing orthotopic GBM. Our study demonstrates that combined treatment with EPIC-1027 and EPIC-1042 induces mitochondrial structural abnormalities and functional impairment, leading to suppressed proliferation and enhanced apoptosis. These findings identified a novel combinatorial therapeutic strategy targeting mitochondria for the treatment of glioblastoma.

title: Liver-specific amino acid metabolism impacts on efficacy of cancer immunotherapy
abstract: Abstract The combination immunotherapies, including those with atezolizumab and bevacizumab (Atez/Bev), have become standard therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, its efficacy remains limited and reliable biomarkers are lacking. In this study, we analyzed paired tumor and background liver tissues from Atez/Bev-treated HCC patients and found that high programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) expression in CD8 + tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) correlated with therapeutic response independent of etiology. RNA sequencing on the tumor samples revealed that the branched-chain amino acid (BCAA)-related metabolic pathway was enriched in the group with high PD-1 expression in CD8⁺ TILs. Along with in vitro experiments, we identified the importance of BCAAs for activation and differentiation of CD8 + T cells. In addition, BCAA metabolism was related to response to PD-1 blockade in not subcutaneous but intrahepatic mouse model–specific manner. Actually, public dataset analyses revealed that high expression of BCAT1 , a key enzyme in BCAA metabolism, was associated with poor prognosis in HCC, but not in other cancer types. These findings suggest the importance of liver-specific BCAA metabolism in antitumor immunity and highlight the need to assess the tumor microenvironment within its organ-specific metabolic context.

title: Phosphorylation of IRS4 at YY111/112 promotes LUSC progression via PI3K/AKT pathway activation
abstract: Abstract Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) lacks effective targeted therapies despite frequent hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway, and the contribution of adaptor proteins to this process remains poorly defined. Here, we identify Insulin Receptor Substrate 4 (IRS4) as a common substrate of Src kinase and the phosphatase RPTPα, and uncover a previously unrecognized, conserved phosphorylation site at YY111/112 within the IRS4 PH domain. Src-mediated phosphorylation at this site is essential for IRS4-driven proliferation, anchorage-independent growth, and invasiveness in LUSC cells. Mechanistically, phosphorylation at YY111/112 induces conformational rearrangements in IRS4 that enhance the recruitment of the p85β SH2 domain to the YXXM motif of IRS4, thereby promoting AKT activation without altering IRS4 protein stability or subcellular distribution. An IRS4-derived cell-permeable phosphopeptide containing pYY111/112 disrupts the Src–IRS4 interaction and significantly suppresses tumor growth in vivo in a YY111/112-dependent manner. Consistently, YY111/112 phosphorylation is markedly elevated in human LUSC tissues and correlates with advanced disease stages. Collectively, these findings define a Src–IRS4–PI3K/AKT signaling axis and identify YY111/112 as a critical regulatory site of IRS4 and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in LUSC

title: Activation of the endocytosis pathway stratifies subtypes and therapeutic sensitivity in colorectal cancer
abstract: Abstract Endocytosis regulates receptor trafficking and signaling, yet its role in colorectal cancer (CRC) remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomic data from 15,025 CRC tumors to evaluate gene expression in clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) and the endosomal sorting complexes required for transport (ESCRT) pathway. Pathway-level signatures were compared across consensus molecular subtypes (CMS) and examined in relation to oncogenic signaling programs, while individual endocytosis-related genes were evaluated for associations with clinical outcomes in an independent randomized trial cohort. Expression of CME and ESCRT pathways varied by CMS, with the highest expression in CMS4 and the lowest in CMS3. Endocytosis signatures correlated with multiple oncogenic signaling pathways, including MAPK, TGF-β, WNT, PI3K, NOTCH, and angiogenesis, suggesting broad links between endocytic activity and tumor biology. In the randomized phase III CALGB/SWOG 80405 trial, low expression of AP2M1 —a core adaptor in the CME complex—was significantly associated with longer overall survival and progression-free survival in patients treated with anti-EGFR agents, but not in those receiving anti-VEGF agents. These findings suggest that endocytic trafficking may be associated with oncogenic signaling and differential therapeutic benefit in patients with metastatic CRC. The endocytosis pathway reflects biologically relevant heterogeneity in CRC and may help guide therapeutic stratification.

title: Fatty acid 2-hydroxylation restrains gastric cancer by blocking CD36 palmitoylation and fatty acid uptake
abstract: Fatty acid (FA)-induced internalization of the FA transporter CD36 normally functions as an intrinsic brake on FA uptake and lipid overload, but cancer cells can bypass this checkpoint to sustain lipid-fueled growth. The mechanism underlying this failure remains unclear. Here, we identify a FA 2-hydroxylase (FA2H)-CD36 signaling axis that operates as an endogenous brake on lipid fueling in gastric cancer cells. FA2H-derived (R)-2-hydroxy palmitic acid ((R)-2-OHPA) disrupts CD36 interaction with its palmitoyltransferase DHHC4, thereby limiting CD36 palmitoylation and trafficking to the plasma membrane. Loss of FA2H permits CD36 palmitoylation and establishes a feed-forward loop that amplifies FA uptake, lipid accumulation, and tumor growth. Restoring FA2H expression or supplementing cells with exogenous (R)-2-OHPA reinstates the lipid-sensing checkpoint. Moreover, FA2H activation sensitizes gastric cancer cells to inhibition of endogenous FA synthesis through blockade of FA synthase (FASN) or stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1). In vivo, (R)-2-OHPA treatment or expression of the palmitoylation-deficient CD36 AASS mutant attenuates FA2H deficiency-driven lipid accumulation and tumor growth, positioning CD36 palmitoylation as the critical effector in this metabolic circuit. Together, these findings establish FA 2-hydroxylation as a metabolic checkpoint that links FA structure to CD36 trafficking and FA utilization in gastric cancer, revealing a targetable vulnerability in lipid-driven tumor growth.

title: Correction: MEF2A transcriptionally upregulates the expression of ZEB2 and CTNNB1 in colorectal cancer to promote tumor progression
FATP5 loss in hepatocellular carcinoma cells orchestrates tumor-promoting microenvironment by inducing passive long-chain fatty acid accumulation within tumor-associated endothelial cells
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by severe immunosuppression and metabolic reprogramming, yet the spatial dynamics of lipid flux between malignant and stromal cells remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a profound, type-specific metabolic rewiring in HCC driven by the widespread downregulation of fatty acid transport protein 5 (FATP5). FATP5 deficiency in malignant cells selectively attenuates the uptake of long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs), creating an extracellular lipid surplus that is passively sequestered by neighboring FATP3-expressing tumor-associated endothelial cells (TECs). Within TECs, accumulated LCFAs function as endogenous ligands that activate the nuclear receptor PPARγ, culminating in the robust transcriptional upregulation and paracrine secretion of the chemokine CXCL12. Endothelial-derived CXCL12 subsequently engages CXCR4 on infiltrating CD8 + T cells, inducing PD-1 expression and driving terminal T-cell exhaustion, thereby establishing an immunosuppressive niche that accelerates tumor progression. Importantly, our data suggest that HCC subtypes marked by FATP5 depletion and CXCL12 + TEC enrichment may possess potential therapeutic susceptibility to PPARγ antagonism or anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade. Besides affecting the secretory function of TECs, accumulated LCFAs can impair endothelial barrier function, thereby creating a microenvironment with hematogenous metastasis risk. Collectively, our findings delineate a novel tumor-promoting microenvironment cascade orchestrated by LCFA spatial redistribution, providing a promising mechanistic foundation to support the future development of targeted precision interventions for FATP5-low HCC.

title: Single‑cell multi‑omics analysis reveals TGF-β1–RUNX2–mediated matCAF differentiation and its role in remodeling the lymph node metastatic microenvironment in bladder cancer
abstract: Lymph node metastasis (LNM) in bladder cancer (BCa) is associated with poor clinical outcomes and may contribute to the development of metastatic tolerance, yet the stromal mechanisms underlying this process remain incompletely understood. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, clinical cohorts, and functional models, we identified an LNM-enriched matrix-remodeling cancer-associated fibroblast (matCAF) state characterized by LRRC15 and POSTN expression and associated with adverse survival and reduced immunotherapy response. Mechanistically, Hybrid_CCND1⁺ malignant epithelial cells promoted matCAF differentiation through FOS-dependent TGFB1 transcription and TGF-β1-TGFBR1-RUNX2 signaling. Spatial analyses further revealed barrier-like accumulation of matCAFs at tumor-stroma interfaces and linked matCAF-rich neighborhoods to enhanced PI3K activity and lymphangiogenesis-related programs. Functionally, matCAF-derived POSTN engaged ITGAV/ITGB5 to activate PI3K-AKT signaling and promote tumor and lymphatic endothelial remodeling. MatCAFs were also associated with SPP1⁺ macrophage remodeling and impaired CD8⁺ T-cell function, partly through RUNX2-associated CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling. Pharmacological disruption of the RUNX2-dependent matCAF program reduced tumor burden and partially restored T-cell activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify matCAF-centered stromal remodeling as a potential cellular basis of the metastatic-tolerance niche in BCa LNM and provide proof-of-concept for therapeutic targeting of the matCAF program.

title: Cancer cell-specific FOXP3 licenses MMP19-dependent matrix remodeling and metastatic dissemination in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a dense desmoplastic stroma and early metastatic dissemination, both of which contribute to its poor prognosis. While forkhead box protein 3 (FOXP3) is best known as a lineage-defining transcription factor in regulatory T cells (Tregs), its aberrant expression in cancer cell-specific FOXP3 (c-FOXP3) may also support tumor-cell-intrinsic progression. Our findings suggest that high c-FOXP3 expression is closely linked to aggressive disease behavior and metastatic progression in PDAC. c-FOXP3 enhanced migration, invasion within three-dimensional collagen-rich matrices, and dissemination in orthotopic models. Integrated transcriptomic analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and wild-type versus binding-site-mutant promoter assays identified matrix metalloproteinase 19 (MMP19) as a direct transcriptional target of c-FOXP3. MMP19 silencing significantly attenuated c-FOXP3-driven migration, matrix invasion, and metastasis. Single-cell sequencing further showed that MMP19 is abundant in cancer-associated fibroblasts but also defines a distinct epithelial pool that is reduced after epithelial Foxp3 deletion. Pharmacological profiling did not identify a validated MMP19-selective inhibitor, whereas the FOXP3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide AZD8701 reduced FOXP3 together with MMP19 mRNA and was accompanied by lower PDAC-cell migration and invasion in vitro. Together, these findings extend the known functions of FOXP3 beyond its classical role in immune tolerance and define a tumor-cell-intrinsic c-FOXP3-MMP19 program that supports matrix-invasive behavior in PDAC and provide preliminary evidence that c-FOXP3 is pharmacologically accessible.

title: Glioma-derived ULBP2 triggers microglial extracellular traps formation via PAD4 lactylation to drive autophagy-dependent malignant growth
abstract: The microglial extracellular traps(MiETs) were appeared in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), but the underlying molecular mechanisms and functions were unknown. In this study, we aimed to explore the ability of GBM-derived UL16-binding protein 2 (ULBP2) on activating MiETs and manipulating microglia to support GBM development. Herein, ULBP2 was identified as a key upregulated protein in GBM and triggered MiETs formation. In turn, MiETs accelerated GBM malignant growth. Mechanistically, GBM released ULBP2 to connect with syndecan-1(SDC1) on microglia, the ULBP2/SDC1 complex induced lactylation of peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4) and following MiETs formation. Furthermore, MiETs stimulated GBM autophagy to promote proliferation and invasion. Our results demonstrated that GBM exerted a crucial role in MiETs formation through the ULBP2/SDC1/PAD4-Kla axis, and the interaction between GBM and microglia created a feed-forward mechanism for tumor progression. Thus, these data provided novel insights into a potential therapeutic target toward MiETs for preventing and suppressing GBM. Glioblastoma(GBM) regulates non-tumor cells in tumor microenvironment to manipulate malignant growth of tumor. In this study, interaction mechanisms between GBM and microglia were investigated. The clinical samples analysis, cellular research and animal experiment were performed. Many biomedical technologies were applied, such as immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence, co-immunoprecipitation, western blot, lentiviral transfection, CCK8, transwell chamber and so on. We found that GBM generated ULBP2 to trigger PAD4-Kla in microglia and following microglial extracellular traps(MiETs). Next, the MiETs contributed to accelerating GBM proliferation and invasion. Our identification supported that GBM-derived ULBP2 participated in crosstalk between GBM and microglia. Furthermore, targeting ULBP2-originated positive feedback pathway between GBM and microglia will be a prominent achievement for GBM treatment.

title: The memory of the tumor microenvironment: epigenetic scarring and the hysteretic logic of therapeutic relapse
abstract: Tumor progression and therapeutic failure are classically interpreted through the lenses of genetic evolution and ongoing signaling dynamics. However, increasing evidence suggests that tumors are also shaped by durable imprints of prior microenvironmental exposures. These prior exposures can leave persistent epigenetic and structural imprints that progressively stabilize adaptive cellular states, allowing transient responses to become durable regulatory programs. Chronic inflammation, metabolic stress, therapeutic pressure, and extracellular matrix remodeling induce persistent molecular states across cancer cells and stromal compartments, generating history-dependent phenotypes that influence future biological responses. Building on these observations, we propose that these adaptive processes collectively constitute a distributed tumor microenvironment (TME) memory encoded across cancer cells, fibroblasts, immune cells, endothelial cells, and the extracellular matrix (ECM), rather than representing isolated mechanisms of adaptation. We examine how TME memory contributes to therapy resistance, immune dysfunction, cancer-cell dormancy, minimal residual disease, and tumor recurrence, and discuss the molecular mechanisms underlying memory encoding, persistence, and recall. Finally, we discuss the experimental and clinical strategies required to identify memory-rich tumors, develop biomarkers of historical imprinting, and design memory-aware therapeutic interventions. By integrating diverse forms of adaptive persistence within a unified history-dependent framework, TME memory provides a conceptual foundation for investigating tumor evolution, therapeutic resistance, and future precision oncology strategies.

title: Paracrine TMSB4X signaling from oligodendrocytes promotes diffuse glioma dissemination
abstract: White matter invasion underlies the lethality of diffuse glioblastoma (GBM), yet its microenvironmental drivers remain poorly defined. Here, we demonstrate that tumor-oligodendrocyte (OL) crosstalk actively promote white matter-associated glioma expansion. In the primary GBM or white matter-invasive glioma, OL lineage cells accumulate at tumor borders and enhance glioma proliferation and migration via secreted factors. Proteomic analysis combined with RNA sequencing identifies OL-derived TMSB4X (thymosin β-4) activates AKT signaling to sustain tumor expansion and invasion. Furthermore, glioma-derived TGF-β stimulates OL differentiation and TMSB4X production, establishing a feed-forward circuit that reinforces tumor progression. Critically, genetic or pharmacological blockade in tumor-OL interaction attenuates glioma outspreading along the white matter in vivo. These findings redefine the OLs as pro-invasive modulators and suggest OL-glioma crosstalk as a therapeutic target in diffuse GBM. Glioblastoma spreads through the brain's white matter while hijacking nearby oligodendrocytes. These cells release TMSB4X, which activates AKT signaling in tumor cells and promotes growth and invasion. In turn, tumors secrete TGF-β, which stimulates oligodendrocytes to produce more TMSB4X. This feed-forward loop may offer a new therapeutic target to prevent glioma from invading the white matter after surgical resection.

title: Stabilization of LTBP2 by SIRT1 promotes EMT and chemosensitivity in cardia gastric adenocarcinoma through TGF-β signaling
abstract: Cardia gastric adenocarcinoma (CGA) is an aggressive malignancy with rising incidence and poor prognosis, driven in part by significant molecular heterogeneity. Through integrated bioinformatics and clinical analyses, we identify Latent-Transforming Growth Factor Beta-Binding Protein 2 (LTBP2) as a key heterogeneously expressed protein markedly upregulated in CGA compared to non-cardia gastric adenocarcinoma (NCGA), correlating with advanced tumor stage and reduced survival. Mechanistically, we uncover a novel post-translational regulation of LTBP2 wherein SIRT1-mediated deacetylation stabilizes LTBP2 by attenuating its binding to the CUL3/SPOP E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, thereby reducing ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Functionally, stabilized LTBP2 activates the TGF-β/PI3K-AKT signaling axis, promoting tumor cell proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and metastasis in vitro and in vivo. Genetic ablation of LTBP2 or SIRT1 impairs tumor growth and EMT, phenotypes rescued by LTBP2 reconstitution. Importantly, LTBP2 deficiency sensitizes tumors to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) chemotherapy, both in cell models and murine xenografts. Collectively, our findings delineate a SIRT1-LTBP2-TGF-β regulatory axis critical for CGA progression and chemoresistance, nominating LTBP2 as a promising therapeutic target in this aggressive gastric cancer subtype.

title: Rethinking therapeutic durability in cancer
abstract: Cancer therapies are commonly evaluated by target inhibition, pathway modulation, or initial tumor response, yet these measures do not reliably predict which treatments produce lasting disease control. Many pharmacodynamically active therapies produce transient benefit followed by relapse, while others achieve therapeutic durability despite comparable initial activity. This Perspective argues that durability is better explained by the behavior of the treated tumor system than by the depth of target suppression and distinguishes three modes of intervention behavior: buffered suppression, in which adaptive escape remains broadly accessible; adaptive constraint, in which future tumor states are narrowed without eradication; and collapse-dominant control, in which treatment drives a state transition that leaves few routes for persistence. Examples from targeted therapy, differentiation therapy, checkpoint blockade, and CAR-T therapy illustrate how the same modality can produce different intervention behaviors depending on tumor biology. A prospective sequence is also proposed for testing which behavior a candidate therapy is likely to induce.

title: Targeting exosomal circSENP5 prevents immune escape of macrophages in pMMR-CRC via regulating mitochondrial metabolism
abstract: Proficient mismatch repair colorectal cancer (pMMR-CRC) exhibits resistance to immunotherapy, presenting a significant clinical challenge that must be addressed. Exosomes, which serve as mediators of intercellular communication, play a crucial role in the tumor microenvironment (TME). However, the mechanisms that exosomes regulate tumor immunity in pMMR-CRC need to be fully elucidated. In this study, we discovered that circSENP5, a circular RNA (circRNA), is highly expressed in pMMR-CRC and is derived from exosomes that are transferred to tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). This transfer enhances the oxidative phosphorylation of macrophages and promotes immunosuppressive characteristics, as well as increased levels of inhibitory receptors on CD8 + T cells. Mechanistically, circSENP5 binds to the deubiquitinase USP10, stabilizing LRPPRC, a key regulator of mitochondrial function. This interaction protects LRPPRC from ubiquitin-mediated degradation, resulting in enhanced mitochondrial respiration and immune suppression. in vivo, the overexpression of circSENP5 accelerates tumor progression, while its mutation disrupts the interaction with USP10, leading to reduced TAM infiltration and improved CD8 + T cell function. Targeting circSENP5 in combination with anti-PD-L1 immune checkpoint therapy effectively suppresses tumor progression, highlighting a potential therapeutic strategy. These findings suggest that exosomal circSENP5 plays a pivotal role in immune evasion in pMMR-CRC by modulating mitochondrial metabolism in TAMs, thereby providing potential therapeutic targets for overcoming immune resistance in pMMR-CRC.

title: ACK1 inhibition suppresses topoisomerase IIα, causing DNA damage accumulation and cellular senescence in RAS mutant lung cancer cells
abstract: Activated Cdc42-associated kinase 1 (ACK1; encoded by the TNK2 gene) is an oncogenic protein of the non-receptor tyrosine kinase family and functions downstream of RAS and activated transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which constitutes around 85% of lung cancer cases, often exhibits amplification or overexpression of the TNK2 gene. This study focuses on demonstrating the therapeutic potential of targeting ACK1 for the treatment of NSCLC. The small molecule ACK1 inhibitor, (R)-9b, preferentially inhibited the growth of NSCLC cell lines possessing activated ACK1, which often have RAS mutations. (R)-9b induced G2/M arrest and robust cellular senescence primarily in the sensitive RAS mutant NSCLC cell lines; these effects were confirmed with ACK1 knockdown. (R)-9b significantly inhibited the growth of both cell line-derived and patient-derived NSCLC xenografts with RAS mutations in vivo. Mechanistically, ACK1 inhibition suppresses topoisomerase 2A (Topo IIα; encoded by TOP2A) expression, along with downregulation of the expression of gene sets associated with the regulation of DNA repair and replication, resulting in accumulation of DNA damage and subsequent cellular senescence. Overall, RAS mutation in NSCLC cell lines activates the Cdc42/ACK1 axis, conferring sensitivity to ACK1 inhibition that causes accumulation of DNA damage via inhibition of Topo IIα and DNA repair, G2/M arrest, and eventual cellular senescence in RAS mutant NSCLC cells.

title: IL-36γ/IL-36R axis reprograms cancer-associated fibroblasts to promote OSCC invasion via ERK1/2-CCL20-mediated ECM remodeling
abstract: The IL-36γ/IL-36R signaling axis mediates cellular communication in various contexts and has recently been implicated in pro-fibrotic responses. However, its specific role in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), which is characterized by abundant cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), remains elusive. Here, we investigated the contribution of IL-36γ/IL-36R signaling to CAF function and OSCC progression. Immunohistochemical analysis of patient samples revealed that IL-36γ was highly expressed in CAFs and that higher co-expression of IL-36γ/IL-36R in CAFs was associated with more invasive patterns and shorter disease-free survival. By integrating tumor cell lines with patient-derived organoids (PDOs), we established three co-culture systems to model these interactions. These models revealed that IL-36γ signaling enhanced CAF proliferation and extracellular matrix remodeling. Mechanistically, the IL-36γ/IL-36R axis in CAFs increased ERK1/2-dependent CCL20 secretion, which in turn promoted tumor cell invasion. Pharmacological blockade of IL-36R attenuated both the IL-36γ-induced increase in CAF abundance and the associated pro-tumorigenic CAF phenotypes in vivo. Collectively, these findings suggest that the IL-36γ/IL-36R-ERK1/2-CCL20 signaling cascade participates in CAF-tumor interactions. Targeting IL-36R may therefore represent a promising therapeutic strategy for invasive OSCC.

title: Dual mTORC1/2 and Scd1 inhibition uncovers a therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer
abstract: Abstract Hyperactivation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, is common in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). However, clinical use of mTOR inhibitors has shown limited efficacy due to rapid adaptive resistance. Using inducible genetically engineered mouse models and matched organoids, we delineated distinct complex-specific adaptations. Loss of mTORC1 delayed tumor progression but induced compensatory PI3K/Akt signalling hyperactivation, while concurrently suppressing inflammatory cancer-associated fibroblasts and desmoplasia through Il-1ra. In contrast, mTORC2 loss impaired de novo sphingolipid synthesis, shifted lipid composition toward saturation, increased the saturated-to-monounsaturated fatty acid ratio, enriched plasma membrane lipid rafts, and amplified interferon-γ signaling. This lipid reprogramming generated a synthetic-lethal dependency on stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (Scd1). Pharmacological co-inhibition of mTORC1/2 and Scd1 prevented adaptive PI3K/Akt signalling rebound, remodelled the tumor stroma, enhanced interferon-γ responses, and synergized with anti-PD-1 therapy. These findings establish dual targeting of mTOR signaling and Scd1 as a rational therapeutic strategy for PDAC.

title: KDM1A promotes colorectal cancer progression by regulating NRP2 and VEGFA-related signaling
abstract: Metastatic progression is a major cause of colorectal cancer (CRC)-related mortality, but the molecular mechanisms underlying this process remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of lysine-specific demethylase 1A (KDM1A) in CRC metastasis and angiogenesis-related phenotypes. Using transcriptomic profiling, chromatin immunoprecipitation, functional assays, and preclinical models, we found that KDM1A contributes to CRC cell migration, invasion, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), with NRP2 upregulation serving as an important associated mechanism. Mechanistically, KDM1A was associated with reduced enrichment of H3K9me1/2 at the NRP2 regulatory region, supporting a chromatin-associated mechanism for NRP2 transcriptional regulation. TGF-β/Smad signaling may also provide an auxiliary input to NRP2 expression. In parallel, KDM1A increased hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) protein stability and VEGFA expression, thereby contributing to angiogenesis-related activity. Our data further suggest that NRP2 and VEGFA-related signaling are linked to PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activation and metastatic phenotypes in CRC cells. Pharmacological inhibition of KDM1A with GSK-LSD1 reduced liver metastatic burden and vascularization within metastatic lesions in preclinical models. Together, these findings suggest that KDM1A contributes to CRC metastatic progression through related mechanisms involving NRP2 regulation, HIF-1α/VEGFA-associated angiogenesis, and AKT pathway modulation, providing a basis for further investigation of KDM1A as a potential therapeutic target in metastatic CRC.

title: SIRT3 deficiency triggers mitochondrial dysfunction-associated senescence to suppress colorectal cancer progression via SLC25A13 acetylation
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is frequently well-known to induce mitochondrial dysfunction-associated senescence (MIDAS), a specialized form of cellular senescence marked by a distinct senescent phenotype. Sirtuin-3 (SIRT3) is a key regulator of mitochondrial function through its deacetylase activity, and emerging evidence highlights that its deficiency induces MIDAS in fibroblasts. However, the precise mechanism by which SIRT3 regulates MIDAS, as well as the role of MIDAS in tumorigenesis, remains incompletely understood. Here, we report that SIRT3 deficiency inhibits colorectal cancer (CRC) progression by inducing MIDAS. Mechanistically, SIRT3 deacetylates the mitochondrial carrier SLC25A13 at lysine 568. SIRT3 loss triggers K568 hyperacetylation, impairing SLC25A13 function and disrupting the malate-aspartate shuttle. This cascade reduces the cytosolic NAD + /NADH ratio, activating the AMPK-p53 axis to initiate MIDAS. Clinically, low levels of SLC25A13-K568 acetylation are associated with poor prognosis in human CRC. Furthermore, senolytic treatment selectively eliminates these senescent cells and suppresses tumor growth. Our findings unveil a SIRT3-SLC25A13 axis governing NAD + /NADH homeostasis and MIDAS, revealing a potential therapeutic strategy for CRC.

title: The FKBPL-RPA1 axis regulates DNA damage repair and cellular survival in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, highlighting the need to identify molecular mechanisms that support tumour cell survival and therapeutic resistance. Here, we identify FK506-binding protein-like (FKBPL) as a novel regulator of the DNA damage repair (DDRR) in HCC. Analysis of public datasets and an HCC tissue microarray demonstrated that FKBPL expression is significantly elevated in HCC tissues compared with normal liver and is associated with poor patient prognosis. Functional studies demonstrate that loss of FKBPL suppresses HCC cell viability and clonogenic survival in vitro and significantly impairs tumour growth in both subcutaneous and orthotopic HCC xenograft models. Transcriptomic analysis following FKBPL knockdown identified marked downregulation of pathways involved in DNA replication and DNA repair. FKBPL knockdown in HCC cell models resulted in increased DNA damage accumulation, activation of ATM/ATR-dependent DNA damage signalling, and enhanced DNA damage accumulation in response to chemotherapy-induced genotoxic stress, whereas FKBPL overexpression reduced DNA damage accumulation in response to genotoxic stress. Replication protein A1 (RPA1), a key regulator of DNA replication and DDRR, was identified as a novel interacting partner of FKBPL. FKBPL physically associated with RPA1 and maintained its protein stability by preventing ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation, thereby supporting downstream BRCA1 signalling and DNA repair. Collectively, these findings establish FKBPL as a previously unrecognised regulator of the DDRR and identify the FKBPL-RPA1 axis as a key mediator of DNA repair and cellular survival in HCC.

title: Early temporal transcriptional and cytokine responses distinguish chemotherapy sensitivity in patient-derived xenograft models of triple-negative breast cancer
abstract: Chemotherapy remains the backbone of neoadjuvant treatment for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), and response to chemotherapy strongly correlates with patient prognosis. However, predicting chemoresistance remains a major clinical challenge. To address this obstacle, we performed serial fine needle aspirations followed by RNA-sequencing on patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models of TNBC that were either chemoresponsive or chemoresistant. We found that these two classes of PDX models exhibited distinct transcriptional trajectories that diverged within one week of chemotherapy initiation, preceding measurable changes in tumor volume. At early time points, chemoresponsive tumors showed activation of apoptotic and cytokine-related pathways, while these changes were absent in chemoresistant models. Notably, cytokine upregulation in chemoresponsive tumors coincided with infiltration of myeloid-derived immune cells into the tumor bed within seven days of chemotherapy, indicating active microenvironment remodeling, even in mice lacking a fully intact immune system. Analysis of paired biopsies from patients with TNBC collected before treatment and within four days of the first chemotherapy dose revealed a consistent pattern: chemoresponsive tumors upregulated inflammatory pathways, whereas chemoresistant tumors showed diminished activation of these pathways. These results underscore the potential clinical value of early on-treatment tumor sampling to detect chemoresistance and guide therapeutic intervention.

title: Disassembly of PKA holoenzyme organization marks prostate cancer progression
abstract: Abstract Prostate cancer is a spatially heterogeneous disease in which signaling transitions driving progression remain poorly defined, because bulk molecular analyses obscure compartment-specific pathway alterations. To resolve spatial signaling organization within human tumors, we performed intra-patient, lesion-matched profiling of MRI-targeted biopsies from the same prostate, focusing on Protein Kinase A (PKA). Immunofluorescence across healthy, Grade Group 1, and Grade Group 4 tissues revealed progressive redistribution of PKA subunits: RIβ expression declined with basal layer disruption, whereas PKAC was redistributed to proliferating tumor cells, establishing a grade-dependent imbalance between regulatory and catalytic components. This redistribution was associated with increased phosphorylation of PKA substrates, linking subunit distribution to pathway activation. Quantitative image analysis and biochemical validation of matched suspicious and non-suspicious biopsy cores from 40 patients confirmed coordinated changes in subunit expression and elevated pathway activity. Analysis of independent proteomics datasets comprising over 400 cases further supported dysregulation of catalytic-to-regulatory PKA balance and revealed enrichment of PKA phosphorylation motifs among recurrence-associated proteins. Together, these findings define a spatial transition in PKA regulatory control and support a model in which spatial redistribution of signaling components contributes to pathway activation in heterogeneous tumors.

title: Therapy-induced tumour senescence drives oxaliplatin resistance via ADORA1–dependent palmitic acid metabolic reprogramming in colorectal cancer
abstract: Oxaliplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) is increasingly used in locally advanced colorectal cancer (CRC); however, early acquired resistance substantially limits its efficacy. We revealed an enrichment of therapy-induced senescence (TIS)-like phenotypes in short-term oxaliplatin-exposed CRC. Consistently, a similar upregulation of senescence markers was observed in oxaliplatin-resistant CRC cells. Senolytic treatment attenuated senescence features and restored oxaliplatin sensitivity in vitro and in vivo. Integrative analysis of RNA-sequencing data from resistant tumours and ABT263-treated resistant tumours identified adenosine A1 receptor (ADORA1) as a key mediator of senescence and oxaliplatin resistance. ADORA1 is highly expressed in CRC tumours and is further induced by oxaliplatin, with elevated ADORA1 levels enriched in chemoresistant patients and associated with poor outcomes following chemotherapy. Mechanistically, ADORA1 directly interacts with and stabilises fatty acid synthase (FASN) by suppressing its ubiquitin-mediated degradation, thereby promoting palmitic acid (PA) synthesis, lipid droplet accumulation and p53/p21-driven senescence. Conversely, ADORA1 knockdown attenuates these phenotypes and restores oxaliplatin sensitivity. Together, these findings identify the ADORA1–FASN–PA metabolic reprogramming as a central mechanistic link between TIS and oxaliplatin resistance in CRC, highlighting this pathway as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming early acquired resistance.
